urv-d2-conditional-continuous.intro: Conditioning restricts the possible losses and rescales the density on the remaining region.
objectives: Normalize a density after conditioning.
Use survival functions and distinguish truncation from a deductible.

sections.title: Restrict and normalize
paragraphs: For an event $A$ with positive probability, $P(B\mid A)=P(B\cap A)/P(A)$. For $a<X<b$, the conditional density is $f_X(x)/(F(b)-F(a))$ on $(a,b)$ and zero elsewhere.
$$P(X>t\mid X>d)=\frac{S(t)}{S(d)},\qquad t\ge d,\quad S(x)=1-F(x).$$

sections.title: Worked example: a reported loss
paragraphs: A loss has density $f(x)=2x$ on $(0,1)$. Given that the loss exceeds $0.5$, find the probability it exceeds $0.8$.

sections.title: Conditional expectation
paragraphs: $$E[g(X)\mid X>d]=\frac{\int_d^\infty g(x)f_X(x)\,dx}{S(d)}.$$
Use the original loss for a loss conditional on a claim. Use $g(x)=x-d$ for the payment above an ordinary deductible.

sections.title: Memorylessness
paragraphs: If $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$, then $P(X>d+t\mid X>d)=e^{-\lambda t}$. The excess $X-d$ conditional on $X>d$ has the original exponential distribution. This property does not hold for every continuous distribution.

urv-d2-conditional-continuous.tip: An unconditional payment includes zero payments. A payment conditional on being positive does not.

urv-e1-expected-value.intro: Expected value is a probability-weighted average. For insurance, it describes long-run average cost, rather than the most likely individual loss.
objectives: Compute discrete and continuous expectations.
Apply LOTUS and linearity to functions of a loss.

sections.title: Discrete and continuous averages
paragraphs: $$E[X]=\sum_x x p_X(x),\qquad E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x f_X(x)\,dx.$$
Check that the relevant absolute integral or sum is finite. An expectation need not be a possible observed value.

sections.title: Functions of a variable: LOTUS
paragraphs: $$E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x)\quad\text{or}\quad \int g(x)f_X(x)\,dx.$$
You can compute a payment expectation directly from the original loss without first deriving its distribution.

sections.title: Worked example: benefit schedule
paragraphs: A loss takes values $0,100,300$ with probabilities $0.5,0.3,0.2$. A policy pays $g(X)=\max(X-100,0)$.
$E[X]=90$, but $E[g(X)]=0(0.5)+0(0.3)+200(0.2)=40$. Applying the deductible to the mean would give zero and is incorrect.

sections.title: Linearity and indicators
paragraphs: $E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c$ even if the variables are dependent. For an indicator $I_A$, $E[I_A]=P(A)$.
For nonnegative $X$, the tail identity $E[X]=\int_0^\infty P(X>t)\,dt$ is often convenient for capped payments.

urv-e1-expected-value.tip: In general, $E[g(X)]\ne g(E[X])$. Linearity applies to sums, not arbitrary nonlinear functions.

urv-e2-moments.intro: Moments summarize location, spread, and shape. Exam calculations often need only the first and second raw moments.
objectives: Compute raw and central moments.
Use second moments for nonlinear benefits and variance.

sections.title: Raw and central moments
paragraphs: The $k$th raw moment is $E[X^k]$. The $k$th central moment is $E[(X-E[X])^k]$. The first central moment is zero; the second is variance.
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2.$$

sections.title: Worked example: a polynomial density
paragraphs: Let $f(x)=2x$ for $0<x<1$. Then $E[X^k]=\int_0^1 2x^{k+1}\,dx=2/(k+2)$ for nonnegative integer $k$.

sections.title: A transformed second moment
paragraphs: For a squared loss benefit, use the second raw moment. For its variance, you will also need the fourth raw moment.

sections.title: Distribution shortcuts
paragraphs: For an exponential variable with mean $\theta$, $E[X^k]=k!\theta^k$. For a gamma variable with shape $\alpha$ and scale $\theta$, $E[X^k]=\theta^k\Gamma(\alpha+k)/\Gamma(\alpha)$. Always identify whether the second parameter is rate or scale.

urv-e2-moments.tip: Calculate the raw second moment first, then subtract the square of the mean. Moment generating functions are extra material, not a requirement of this syllabus.

urv-e3-mode-median-percentiles.intro: The mean, mode, and median answer different questions. Percentiles identify loss thresholds exceeded with a specified probability.
objectives: Find modes from PMFs or densities.
Calculate quantiles for discrete and continuous variables.

sections.title: Modes
paragraphs: A discrete mode maximizes $p_X(x)$. A continuous mode maximizes $f_X(x)$ on its support. Check endpoints and ties as well as stationary points.
For $f(x)=6x(1-x)$ on $(0,1)$, $f\prime(x)=6-12x$; the mode is $1/2$.

sections.title: Median and percentiles
paragraphs: The lower $p$-quantile is $q_p=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge p\}$. For a continuous strictly increasing CDF, solve $F(q_p)=p$. A median has at least half the probability on either side.

sections.title: Worked example: exponential threshold
paragraphs: For an exponential loss with mean $1000$, $F(x)=1-e^{-x/1000}$. Its median is $1000\ln 2\approx693.15$, and its 90th percentile is $-1000\ln(0.1)\approx2302.59$.

sections.title: Discrete percentiles
paragraphs: If $P(X=0)=0.3$, $P(X=1)=0.4$, and $P(X=2)=0.3$, the lower 60th percentile is $1$, since $F(0)=0.3<0.6\le F(1)=0.7$. Do not interpolate between discrete values unless explicitly instructed.

urv-e3-mode-median-percentiles.tip: A 95th percentile leaves 5% in the upper tail. Convert the wording into a CDF probability before solving.

urv-f1-variance.intro: Variance measures squared deviations around the mean. Its units are the square of the loss units.
objectives: Compute variance from raw moments.
Scale variance and recognize constant shifts.

sections.title: Two equivalent definitions
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]=E[X^2]-\mu^2,\qquad\mu=E[X].$$
Variance is nonnegative and is zero for a constant random variable.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A loss is $0,100,300$ with probabilities $0.5,0.3,0.2$. Its mean is $90$ and second moment is $10000(0.3)+90000(0.2)=21000$.
The variance is $21000-90^2=12900$.

sections.title: Scaling and shifting
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).$$
Adding a fixed fee changes the mean, but not variance. Doubling every loss quadruples variance.

sections.title: Sums
paragraphs: For independent variables, $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. For dependent variables, add $2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$. Independence is not needed for means to add.

urv-f1-variance.tip: Keep full precision for both raw moments before subtracting. A negative variance indicates an error or excessive rounding.

urv-f2-standard-deviation.intro: Standard deviation converts squared spread back into the original units, making loss variability easier to interpret.
objectives: Calculate standard deviation.
Transform standard deviation and distinguish it from the standard deviation of an average.

sections.title: Definition and units
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.$$
If losses are measured in dollars, variance is in squared dollars and standard deviation is in dollars.

sections.title: Transformations
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{SD}(aX+b)=|a|\operatorname{SD}(X).$$
If $\operatorname{Var}(X)=400$ and $Y=3X-100$, then $\operatorname{SD}(Y)=3\sqrt{400}=60$.

sections.title: Independent sums and averages
paragraphs: For $n$ independent variables with the same variance $\sigma^2$, the sum has standard deviation $\sigma\sqrt n$ and the average has standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

sections.title: Worked example: aggregate claims
paragraphs: For $100$ independent claims each with standard deviation $200$, the total standard deviation is $2000$, while the average claim standard deviation is $20$. Adding the $100$ individual standard deviations would be incorrect.

urv-f2-standard-deviation.tip: In $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, the second parameter is variance. Take its square root when standardizing.

urv-f3-coefficient-variation.intro: The coefficient of variation compares spread relative to the mean, useful when portfolios have different average costs.
objectives: Compute and interpret CV.
Understand the effect of scaling and shifting losses.

sections.title: Definition
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{CV}(X)=\frac{\operatorname{SD}(X)}{E[X]},\qquad E[X]>0.$$
CV is dimensionless. For positive losses, a CV of 0.5 means the standard deviation is half the mean.

sections.title: Scale invariance
paragraphs: For $a>0$, $\operatorname{CV}(aX)=\operatorname{CV}(X)$. A shift does change CV: $\operatorname{CV}(X+b)=\sigma/(\mu+b)$ when the denominator is positive.

sections.title: Worked example: gamma parameters
paragraphs: A gamma loss with shape $\alpha$ and scale $\theta$ has mean $\alpha\theta$, variance $\alpha\theta^2$, and CV $1/\sqrt\alpha$. A CV of $0.5$ implies $\alpha=4$.

sections.title: Pooling independent risks
paragraphs: For $n$ i.i.d. nonnegative losses with positive mean, $\operatorname{CV}(\sum X_i)=\operatorname{CV}(X_1)/\sqrt n$. Pooling independent risks reduces relative variability, although total standard deviation increases.

urv-f3-coefficient-variation.tip: CV is not variance divided by the mean. It uses standard deviation; a zero mean makes this definition undefined.

urv-g1-deductibles.intro: An ordinary deductible makes the policyholder pay the first portion of each covered loss. A franchise deductible uses a different payment rule.
objectives: Build payment functions for ordinary and franchise deductibles.
Calculate payment probabilities and expected payments.

sections.title: Ordinary deductible
paragraphs: There is a probability mass at zero: $P(Y=0)=P(X\le d)$. For $y\ge0$, $F_Y(y)=F_X(d+y)$; for $y<0$, $F_Y(y)=0$.

sections.title: Franchise deductible
paragraphs: Under the convention that payment occurs only when $X>d$, a franchise policy pays $Y=X\,I_{\{X>d\}}$. An ordinary policy pays only the excess above $d$. State the convention at equality for a discrete loss.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: With loss $1500$ and deductible $500$, an ordinary policy pays $1000$; a franchise policy pays the full $1500$. Both pay zero for loss $400$.

sections.title: Expected payment
paragraphs: $$E[(X-d)_+]=\int_d^\infty S_X(x)\,dx.$$
For an exponential loss of mean $\theta$, $E[Y]=\theta e^{-d/\theta}$. This expectation includes losses that produce no payment.

urv-g1-deductibles.tip: A deductible truncates the payment amount; it does not simply condition the original loss distribution.

urv-g2-coinsurance.intro: Coinsurance specifies what fraction of a covered loss the insurer pays. Identify whose percentage is being stated.
objectives: Translate coinsurance wording into a payment.
Scale payment means and variances.

sections.title: Insurer share
paragraphs: If the insurer pays a proportion $c$ after an ordinary deductible, $Y=c(X-d)_+$, where $0\le c\le1$. If the policyholder pays 20%, the insurer share is 80%.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A loss is $5000$, the ordinary deductible is $1000$, and the insurer pays 75% of the remaining loss. Payment is $0.75(5000-1000)=3000$. The policyholder retains $2000$ in total.

sections.title: Moments
paragraphs: $$E[cY_0]=cE[Y_0],\qquad \operatorname{Var}(cY_0)=c^2\operatorname{Var}(Y_0).$$
If $Y_0$ has mean $600$ and variance $90000$, a 70% share gives mean $420$, variance $44100$, and standard deviation $210$.

sections.title: Order of operations
paragraphs: A cap of $u$ on the insurer payment gives $Y=\min(c(X-d)_+,u)$. A cap of $u$ on the covered amount before coinsurance gives $Y=c\min((X-d)_+,u)$. These are different contracts.

urv-g2-coinsurance.tip: Write the contract as one function before substituting the loss. The location of a cap relative to coinsurance matters.

urv-g3-benefit-limits.intro: A benefit limit caps what the insurer pays. Capping creates probability mass at the maximum payment.
objectives: Distinguish a payment limit from a loss limit.
Calculate probabilities and moments of capped payments.

sections.title: Payment cap
paragraphs: With ordinary deductible $d$ and maximum insurer payment $u$, $Y=\min((X-d)_+,u)$. Payment is zero below $d$, $X-d$ between $d$ and $d+u$, and $u$ above $d+u$.

sections.title: Distribution and point masses
paragraphs: $P(Y=0)=F_X(d)$ and $P(Y=u)=P(X\ge d+u)$. For a continuous loss the latter is $S_X(d+u)$. For $0\le y<u$, $F_Y(y)=F_X(d+y)$; for $y\ge u$, $F_Y(y)=1$.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: A policy has deductible $200$ and payment cap $500$. A loss of $900$ produces payment $500$, not $700$. For $X$ uniform on $(0,1000)$, the payment has mass $0.2$ at zero and $0.3$ at $500$.

sections.title: Tail integration
paragraphs: $$E[Y]=\int_d^{d+u}S_X(x)\,dx,\qquad E[Y^2]=2\int_0^u y S_X(d+y)\,dy.$$
For the uniform example, $E[Y]=\int_{200}^{700}(1-x/1000)\,dx=275$. A limit $L$ on covered loss instead yields payment $\max(\min(X,L)-d,0)$, whose maximum is $(L-d)_+$.

urv-g3-benefit-limits.tip: Check whether the limit caps the original covered loss or the insurer payment. Never ignore the probability mass at the cap.

urv-g4-inflation.intro: Inflation scales the loss before applying fixed policy terms. A fixed deductible changes its relative size after inflation.
objectives: Transform loss distributions under inflation.
Apply inflated losses to deductibles, coinsurance, and caps.

sections.title: Inflated loss
paragraphs: If inflation is $r$, the new loss is $X^*=(1+r)X$. Its mean is $(1+r)E[X]$, variance is $(1+r)^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$, and $F_{X^*}(x)=F_X(x/(1+r))$.

sections.title: Fixed contract terms
paragraphs: Apply inflation first when the deductible and payment cap remain fixed in nominal currency. If the problem says these terms also increase, update them separately.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: The original loss is $1200$. Inflation is 10%, the fixed deductible is $500$, the insurer share is 80%, and the payment cap is $600$. Payment is $\min(0.8(1320-500),600)=600$.

sections.title: Exponential shortcut
paragraphs: If the original loss is exponential with mean $\theta$ and only an ordinary deductible applies, then $E[Y]=(1+r)\theta\exp(-d/((1+r)\theta))$. This is not generally $(1+r)$ times the old payment expectation.

urv-g4-inflation.tip: Inflating a payment after subtracting a fixed deductible gives a different answer from inflating the loss first.

urv-h1-loss-variable.intro: Separate the occurrence of a claim from its severity. A loss random variable may include a substantial chance of no loss.
objectives: Model a loss with a mass at zero.
Compute loss moments for mixtures and retention.

sections.title: Occurrence and severity
paragraphs: Let $I$ be Bernoulli with probability $q$ and let severity $Z$ be independent of $I$. The per-policy loss is $X=IZ$. For positive severities, $P(X=0)=1-q$.

sections.title: Moments of the mixture
paragraphs: $$E[X]=qE[Z],\quad E[X^2]=qE[Z^2],\quad \operatorname{Var}(X)=q\operatorname{Var}(Z)+q(1-q)(E[Z])^2.$$
Severity conditional on a claim is not the same variable as loss per policy.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Claim probability is $0.1$. Conditional severity has mean $1000$ and variance $400000$. Then $E[X]=100$, $E[X^2]=0.1(400000+1000000)=140000$, and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=130000$.

sections.title: Insured and retained loss
paragraphs: If the insurer payment is $Y=g(X)$, the retained loss is $R=X-Y$. Then $E[R]=E[X]-E[Y]$. The variables $X$ and $Y$ are generally dependent, so their variances cannot simply be subtracted.

urv-h1-loss-variable.tip: Determine whether a supplied severity distribution is conditional on a claim or already includes no-claim outcomes.

urv-h2-payment-variable.intro: A policy transforms a loss into an insurer payment. Even a continuous loss can produce a mixed payment distribution.
objectives: Derive the distribution of a payment.
Distinguish payment per loss from payment per payment.

sections.title: Map each loss outcome
paragraphs: For deductible $d$, insurer share $c>0$, and payment cap $u$, write $Y=\min(c(X-d)_+,u)$. On the interior, $X=d+Y/c$.
For $0<y<u$, $f_Y(y)=f_X(d+y/c)/c$. Add masses $P(Y=0)=P(X\le d)$ and $P(Y=u)=P(X\ge d+u/c)$ separately.

sections.title: Per loss versus per payment
paragraphs: $Y$ per loss includes zeros. A payment per payment has the conditional distribution $Y\mid Y>0$. If $q=P(Y>0)>0$, then $E[Y\mid Y>0]=E[Y]/q$.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: For $X$ uniform on $(0,1000)$ and deductible $200$, $P(Y>0)=0.8$ and $E[Y]=320$. Thus the mean positive payment is $320/0.8=400$.

sections.title: Conditional second moment
paragraphs: $E[Y^2\mid Y>0]=E[Y^2]/q$. Subtract $(E[Y]/q)^2$ to obtain the conditional variance. Dividing the unconditional variance by $q$ alone does not work.

urv-h2-payment-variable.tip: A payment PDF over positive amounts may integrate to less than one. The missing probability belongs to zero and any capped payment.

urv-h3-moments-loss-payment.intro: Calculate payment moments by applying the policy to the loss inside the expectation. Keep zero and capped outcomes in the calculation.
objectives: Compute first and second payment moments.
Calculate conditional payment variance and standard deviation.

sections.title: Direct method
paragraphs: $$E[Y^k]=E[g(X)^k]=\sum_x g(x)^k p_X(x)\quad\text{or}\quad\int g(x)^k f_X(x)\,dx.$$
For $Y=\min((X-d)_+,u)$ and a continuous loss, $E[Y^k]=\int_d^{d+u}(x-d)^k f_X(x)\,dx+u^kP(X\ge d+u)$ for $k>0$.

sections.title: Worked example: uniform loss
paragraphs: $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=170666.67-320^2=68266.67$, so $\operatorname{SD}(Y)\approx261.28$. The original loss has mean $500$ and variance $1000^2/12$.

sections.title: Exponential deductible
paragraphs: For exponential loss with mean $\theta$, $E[Y]=\theta e^{-d/\theta}$ and $E[Y^2]=2\theta^2e^{-d/\theta}$. Subtract the squared mean for variance.

sections.title: Positive payments
paragraphs: If $q=P(Y>0)$, then $\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid Y>0)=E[Y^2]/q-(E[Y]/q)^2$. For the uniform example, the positive payment is uniform on $(0,800)$, with variance $800^2/12$.

urv-h3-moments-loss-payment.tip: The second moment is not the variance. For a cap, include the cap amount raised to the relevant power times its probability.

mrv-a1-joint-distributions.intro: A joint PMF assigns probability to each possible pair. Row and column totals recover the individual distributions.
objectives: Normalize a joint PMF and calculate marginals.
Evaluate joint CDFs and check independence.

sections.title: Joint PMF and support
paragraphs: $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y)\ge0$ and $\sum_x\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)=1$. List the support before summing; cells outside it have probability zero.

sections.title: Joint CDF
paragraphs: $$F_{X,Y}(a,b)=P(X\le a,Y\le b)=\sum_{x\le a}\sum_{y\le b}p(x,y).$$
In the example, $F(0.5,0.5)=0.1$ and $F(1,0.5)=0.4$. Rectangle probabilities use inclusion–exclusion: $P(a<X\le b,c<Y\le d)=F(b,d)-F(a,d)-F(b,c)+F(a,c)$.

sections.title: Independence
paragraphs: $X$ and $Y$ are independent exactly when $p(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$ for every pair. In the example, $p(0,0)=0.1\ne0.3(0.4)$, so they are dependent. For independent variables the joint CDF factors as $F_X(a)F_Y(b)$.

mrv-a1-joint-distributions.tip: This syllabus requires discrete joint and conditional calculations. Continuous order statistics and sums of independent normals are covered in their own chapters.

mrv-a2-conditional-distributions.intro: Conditioning on one coordinate reduces the joint table to a row or column and normalizes its entries.
objectives: Calculate discrete conditional PMFs.
Find conditional means and variances from a joint distribution.

sections.title: Conditional PMF
paragraphs: $$p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{p(x,y)}{p_Y(y)},\qquad p_Y(y)>0.$$
Sum the relevant column to get the denominator. The resulting conditional probabilities sum to one.

sections.title: Conditional moments
paragraphs: $$E[g(X)\mid Y=y]=\sum_x g(x)\,p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y).$$
In the example $X\mid Y=1$ is Bernoulli with parameter $2/3$. Its mean is $2/3$, its second moment is $2/3$, and its variance is $2/9$.

sections.title: Independence check
paragraphs: For independent variables, $p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=p_X(x)$ for every conditioning value with positive probability. Checking a single matching row is not enough to establish independence.

mrv-a2-conditional-distributions.tip: Do not divide by the probability of the variable you are trying to find. The denominator is the probability of the condition.

mrv-b1-joint-moments.intro: Joint moments summarize the combined behavior of two discrete variables. Marginal and conditional moments use the same weighted-average principle.
objectives: Calculate mixed moments such as E[XY].
Apply total expectation and total variance.

sections.title: Joint moments
paragraphs: $$E[g(X,Y)]=\sum_x\sum_y g(x,y)p(x,y).$$
For a mixed moment, use $g(x,y)=x^r y^s$. You do not need independence to use this formula.

sections.title: Total expectation
paragraphs: $$E[X]=\sum_y E[X\mid Y=y]p_Y(y)=E[E[X\mid Y]].$$

sections.title: Total variance
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]+\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid Y]).$$
The first term is variation within groups; the second is variation between group means. In the worked table these are $5/24$ and $1/600$, totaling $0.21$.

mrv-b1-joint-moments.tip: $E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]$ follows from independence; it is not a general identity for joint distributions.

mrv-b2-conditional-variance.intro: Conditional and marginal distributions describe different populations. Compute the variance using the probability weights for the population specified.
objectives: Find variance and SD from a marginal PMF.
Compute conditional variance and compare it with total variance.

sections.title: Marginal variance
paragraphs: First sum out the other variable to find $p_X(x)$. Then calculate $E[X]$, $E[X^2]$, and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2$.

sections.title: Conditional variance
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y=y)=E[X^2\mid Y=y]-(E[X\mid Y=y])^2.$$
Normalize the conditional PMF before calculating either moment. The conditional standard deviation is the square root of this variance.

sections.title: Worked example
paragraphs: Conditional on $Y=0$, $X$ takes values $0,2$ equally likely. Conditional on $Y=1$, $X=1$ with certainty. Each $Y$ value has probability $1/2$.
Both conditional means are $1$. Conditional variances are $1$ and $0$. Marginal probabilities are $1/4,1/2,1/4$ at $0,1,2$, so the marginal variance is $1/2$ and SD is $1/\sqrt2$.

sections.title: Why conditional variance alone is not enough
paragraphs: The average conditional variance equals the marginal variance only if the conditional mean has zero variance. Otherwise use $E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]+\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid Y])$.

mrv-b2-conditional-variance.tip: A condition can increase or decrease variance. Do not assume conditional variance always shrinks.

mrv-c1-covariance.intro: Covariance measures the direction of linear association. Correlation rescales that association to a dimensionless number between −1 and 1.
objectives: Compute covariance and correlation for discrete variables.
Use covariance in the variance of a linear combination.

sections.title: Covariance
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y].$$
Positive covariance means above-average values tend to occur together; negative covariance means they tend to move in opposite directions.

sections.title: Correlation
paragraphs: $$\rho_{X,Y}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{SD}(X)\operatorname{SD}(Y)}.$$
Correlation is undefined if either variance is zero. Zero correlation does not generally imply independence.

sections.title: Variance of a linear combination
paragraphs: $$\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).$$
For a difference the covariance term is negative: $\operatorname{Var}(X-Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)-2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$.

mrv-c1-covariance.tip: Independence implies zero covariance when the relevant moments exist. The converse is false.

mrv-d1-order-statistics.intro: Order statistics are sample values sorted from smallest to largest. Their distributions describe maximum claims, minimum waiting times, and ranked losses.
objectives: Find probabilities for minima, maxima, and intermediate ranks.
Determine joint distributions of order statistics.

sections.title: Extremes and ranks for i.i.d. samples
paragraphs: For $n$ i.i.d. continuous variables with CDF $F$, $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^n$ and $P(X_{(1)}>x)=(1-F(x))^n$.
$$P(X_{(k)}\le x)=\sum_{j=k}^n\binom nj F(x)^j(1-F(x))^{n-j}.$$
Count how many observations fall below the threshold. The kth smallest is below it exactly when at least k observations are below it.

sections.title: Density and uniform ranks
paragraphs: For uniform $(0,1)$ observations, $X_{(k)}$ is beta with parameters $k,n+1-k$, mean $k/(n+1)$, and variance $k(n+1-k)/((n+1)^2(n+2))$.

sections.title: Joint density of two ranks
paragraphs: For $i<j$ and $x<y$, the joint density for i.i.d. continuous observations is
It is zero for $x\ge y$. Integrate this density over the requested region. The factors count observations before x, between x and y, and after y.

sections.title: Joint distribution of the entire ordered sample
paragraphs: For i.i.d. continuous observations, the joint density of all n order statistics is $n!\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i)$ on $x_1<\cdots<x_n$, and zero otherwise. The factorial counts all assignments of the original observation labels to the ordered positions.

For independent continuous observations with different densities, replace this with $\sum_{\pi}\prod_{i=1}^n f_i(x_{\pi(i)})$, summing over all permutations of the n ordered positions. For two observations, this is $f_1(x)f_2(y)+f_1(y)f_2(x)$ on $x<y$.

For discrete observations, sort each possible original outcome vector and add its probability to the corresponding ordered vector. With two independent Bernoulli(p) observations, the ordered pairs $(0,0),(0,1),(1,1)$ have probabilities $(1-p)^2,2p(1-p),p^2$. The pair $(1,0)$ cannot be ordered.

sections.title: Worked joint probability
paragraphs: For three independent uniform $(0,1)$ observations, the joint minimum–maximum density is $6(y-x)$ for $0<x<y<1$.
The probability that all three fall in $(0.2,0.8)$ is $P(X_{(1)}>0.2,X_{(3)}<0.8)=(0.8-0.2)^3=0.216$.

sections.title: Independent, nonidentical observations
paragraphs: Independence alone gives $F_{\max}(x)=\prod_i F_i(x)$ and $P(\min>x)=\prod_i(1-F_i(x))$. For independent continuous variables with different CDFs, the min–max density on $x<y$ is $\sum_{i\ne j}f_i(x)f_j(y)\prod_{k\ne i,j}(F_k(y)-F_k(x))$.
For discrete samples, ties are possible. Use event counts or enumerate outcomes rather than using the continuous density formulas.

mrv-d1-order-statistics.tip: The second largest of n observations is rank n−1, not rank 2. The beta and binomial rank formulas require identically distributed observations.

mrv-e1-linear-combinations.intro: Linear combinations represent totals, differences, and weighted portfolios. Start with the mean and variance, then identify the distribution.
objectives: Calculate probabilities for independent discrete sums.
Calculate probabilities for linear combinations of independent normals.

sections.title: Discrete convolution
paragraphs: For independent discrete variables, $P(X+Y=s)=\sum_x p_X(x)p_Y(s-x)$. More generally, sum $p_X(x)p_Y(y)$ over all pairs satisfying $ax+by\le t$ to get $P(aX+bY\le t)$.

sections.title: Worked discrete example
paragraphs: Let independent $X,Y$ be Bernoulli with probabilities $0.3,0.4$. For $T=2X+Y$, the probabilities at $0,1,2,3$ are $0.42,0.28,0.18,0.12$, so $P(T\ge2)=0.30$.

sections.title: Distribution shortcuts
paragraphs: Independent Poisson variables sum to Poisson with the summed rate. Independent binomials sum to binomial when they share the same success probability. Different binomial success probabilities do not give this shortcut.

sections.title: Independent normal combination
paragraphs: $$\sum_i a_iX_i+b\sim N\left(\sum_i a_i\mu_i+b,\sum_i a_i^2\sigma_i^2\right).$$
If $X\sim N(100,400)$ and $Y\sim N(80,225)$ are independent, $X-Y\sim N(20,625)$. Thus $P(X>Y)=\Phi(20/25)=\Phi(0.8)\approx0.7881$.

sections.title: Standardizing
paragraphs: For $T\sim N(\mu_T,\sigma_T^2)$, $P(T\le t)=\Phi((t-\mu_T)/\sigma_T)$. Independent normal combinations are exactly normal; no large-sample approximation is needed.

mrv-e1-linear-combinations.tip: Weights are squared in the variance. A negative weight reverses the mean contribution but never creates a negative variance contribution.

mrv-e2-linear-moments.intro: Expectations of linear combinations are linear. Variances use squared weights and, when necessary, covariance terms.
objectives: Compute moments of independent weighted sums.
Distinguish sums, averages, and differences.

sections.title: First moment
paragraphs: $$E[T]=b+\sum_i a_iE[X_i],\qquad T=b+\sum_i a_iX_i.$$
This expectation formula does not require independence.

sections.title: Variance and second raw moment
paragraphs: For independent variables, $\operatorname{Var}(T)=\sum_i a_i^2\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$ and $E[T^2]=\operatorname{Var}(T)+(E[T])^2$. For dependent variables, include $2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$.

sections.title: Worked weighted portfolio
paragraphs: Independent $X,Y$ have means $10,20$ and variances $4,9$. For $T=2X-3Y+5$, the mean is $-35$, variance is $4(4)+9(9)=97$, and second raw moment is $97+1225=1322$.

sections.title: Sample means
paragraphs: For $n$ i.i.d. variables with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, $E[\bar X]=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n$. For a total, mean is $n\mu$ and variance is $n\sigma^2$.

mrv-e2-linear-moments.tip: A constant adds to the mean, contributes zero variance, and still affects the second raw moment through the squared mean.

mrv-f1-central-limit-theorem.intro: The CLT approximates the distribution of a large sum or average of independent, identically distributed variables with finite variance.
objectives: Standardize a sum or sample mean.
Use continuity corrections and recognize approximation limits.

sections.title: Conditions and standardization
paragraphs: Let $X_i$ be i.i.d. with finite mean $\mu$ and finite positive variance $\sigma^2$. For large $n$,
$$\frac{\sum X_i-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\approx N(0,1),\qquad\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\approx N(0,1).$$
The approximation improves as n grows. Strong skewness can require a much larger sample; n=30 is not a guarantee. The CLT does not make each individual observation normal.

sections.title: Worked aggregate loss
paragraphs: For $100$ independent losses with mean $50$ and SD $20$, the total has mean $5000$ and SD $200$. Hence $P(\sum X_i>5400)\approx1-\Phi(2)=0.0228$.

sections.title: Continuity correction
paragraphs: For integer-valued totals, approximate $P(S\le k)$ with $P(N<k+0.5)$ and $P(S\ge k)$ with $P(N>k-0.5)$. For $a\le S\le b$, use the interval from $a-0.5$ to $b+0.5$.
The half-unit correction applies to unit-spaced integer outcomes. For a different lattice spacing, use half that spacing.

sections.title: Binomial example
paragraphs: For $S\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(100,0.5)$, mean is $50$ and SD is $5$. Then $P(45\le S\le55)\approx\Phi(1.1)-\Phi(-1.1)=0.7287$. The endpoints are $44.5$ and $55.5$ after correction.

sections.title: Choosing a method
paragraphs: If the inputs are independent normal variables, the total is exactly normal. For independent discrete variables with small supports, exact convolution is often preferable. Use the CLT for large sums when an approximation is requested or justified.

mrv-f1-central-limit-theorem.tip: Standardize totals with SD times the square root of n; standardize averages with SD divided by the square root of n.
